rewritten_text:
“Are you talking about—Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I am. I could never have meant anyone else, and I thought you knew. It seemed perfectly clear when we discussed him.”

“Not entirely,” Emma replied, forcing herself to sound calm. “Everything you said then seemed to refer to someone different. I could almost swear you mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill by name. I am certain we spoke about his helping you when he protected you from the gypsies.”

“Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how you’ve forgotten!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember the substance of what I said perfectly. I told you your affection did not surprise me, that it was entirely natural considering what he had done for you. You agreed and spoke very warmly about your gratitude for that kindness. You even described how you felt when you saw him coming to rescue you. I remember it vividly.”

“Oh dear,” Harriet exclaimed, “now I understand what you mean. But I had something quite different in mind then. I wasn’t talking about the gypsies or Mr. Frank Churchill. No!” Her tone rose a little. “I was thinking of something far more precious: Mr. Knightley coming to ask me to dance when Mr. Elton refused, and there was no other partner available. That was the kindness, the noble goodness and generosity. That was the service that first made me realize how much better he was than anyone else in the world.”

“Good God!” cried Emma. “This has been a most unfortunate—a truly dreadful misunderstanding! What can we do?”

“Then you wouldn’t have encouraged me if you had understood? Still, at least I can’t be worse off than I would have been if I’d meant the other gentleman. And now—it is possible—”

She paused for a few moments. Emma could not speak.

“I’m not surprised, Miss Woodhouse,” Harriet continued, “that you see a great difference between them, whether for me or for anyone else. You must think one is five hundred million times further above me than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—that if—strange as it may seem— You did say yourself that more extraordinary things had happened, that people with greater differences in rank than Mr. Frank Churchill and I had married. So it seems that even something like this may have happened before. And if I should be fortunate beyond anything I can express—if Mr. Knightley really should—if he doesn’t object to the difference between us, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you won’t oppose it or try to put obstacles in our way.

He made no second attempt. The boys lay counting each slow moment until they felt time must have ended and eternity itself grown old. At last, with relief, they noticed the sun going down.

One of the snores stopped. Injun Joe sat up and looked around. He gave a grim smile at his companion, whose head had sunk onto his knees, then prodded him awake with a foot.

“Hey! Some lookout you are! Still, it’s all right. Nothing happened.”

“Good grief! Was I asleep?”

“Oh, a little. A little. Nearly time to move, partner. What should we do with the bit of loot we have left?”

“I don’t know. Leave it here like always, I suppose. No point taking it until we head south. Six hundred and fifty dollars in silver is a lot to carry.”

“Well, all right. Coming back once more won’t hurt.”

“No, but I’d come at night, like we used to. That’s better.”

“Yes, but listen. It could be a long while before I get the right opportunity for that job. Something might happen, and this isn’t a very safe hiding place. Let’s bury it properly, good and deep.”

“Good idea,” his companion said. He crossed the room, knelt, lifted one of the hearthstones at the back, and pulled out a bag that gave a pleasant jingle. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then passed over the bag. Joe was now kneeling in the corner, digging with his bowie knife.

The boys instantly forgot every fear and discomfort. They followed each movement with greedy eyes. What luck! Its magnificence was beyond imagination. Six hundred dollars could make six boys rich. Here was treasure hunting in the best possible circumstances, without any tiresome uncertainty about where to dig. They kept nudging each other, and every eloquent nudge meant the same easily understood thing: “Aren’t you glad we’re here now!”

Joe’s knife hit something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” asked his companion.

“A half-rotten board. No, I think it’s a box. Here, help me and we’ll see what it’s doing here. Never mind, I’ve made a hole.”

He reached inside and pulled his hand back out.

“Man, it’s money!”

They examined the handful of coins. Gold. The boys above were just as thrilled and delighted as the men.

Joe’s companion said:

“We’ll get this out quickly. There’s an old rusty pick in the weeds at the corner on the other side of the fireplace. I noticed it a minute ago.”

Despite all this, the boy grew steadily paler, sadder, and more dejected. She added hot baths, sitting baths, showers, and cold plunges. He remained as cheerful as a hearse. She supplemented the water with a meager oatmeal diet and plasters designed to raise blisters. Estimating his capacity as though he were a jug, she filled him daily with fraudulent cure-alls.

By now Tom no longer cared about being persecuted. This development alarmed the old lady deeply. His indifference had to be broken, whatever it took. Then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time and immediately ordered a supply. She tasted it and felt profoundly grateful: it was pure liquid fire. She abandoned water treatment and every other remedy, placing all her trust in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and anxiously watched what happened. At once her worries vanished and her soul found peace. His “indifference” was gone. He could hardly have shown more vigorous, wholehearted interest if she had lit a fire beneath him.

Tom decided it was time to take action. This way of living might suit the romance of his blighted existence, but it was becoming short on sentiment and long on unpleasant surprises. He considered several ways to get relief and finally decided to pretend he loved Pain-killer. He asked for it so often that he became a nuisance. Eventually his aunt told him to take it himself and stop bothering her. If Sid had behaved this way, no doubts would have spoiled her pleasure. Since it was Tom, she secretly watched the bottle. The medicine really was disappearing, she saw, but she never imagined that he was using it to improve the health of a crack in the sitting-room floor.

One day, as Tom was treating the crack, his aunt’s yellow cat approached, purring and watching the spoon greedily, begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask unless you really want it, Peter.”

Peter made it clear that he did.

“You’d better be certain.”

Peter was certain.

“All right, you asked, and I’ll give you some, because I’m not stingy. But if you don’t like it, you have nobody to blame but yourself.”

Peter agreed. Tom forced his mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. The cat leaped a couple of yards into the air, let out a battle cry, and raced around and around the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flowerpots, and causing general destruction.
